title: Why Do Humans LAUGH?
title_alternatives: Your Laugh Is 10 Million Years OLD
The Real Reason We LAUGH (It's Not Jokes)
The Town That Couldn't Stop LAUGHING
description:
In 1962, three schoolgirls started laughing and couldn't stop. Weeks later, a school had to close. From tickled apes and laughing rats to a laugh that reveals who your friends are, this is the strange, ancient story of why humans laugh.

This video is history and science for education, not medical advice.

Sources:
- Rankin & Philip (1963). An epidemic of laughing in the Bukoba district of Tanganyika. Central African Journal of Medicine.
- Hempelmann (2007). The laughter of the 1962 Tanganyika 'laughter epidemic'. Humor.
- Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology.
- Panksepp & Burgdorf (2003). 'Laughing' rats and the evolutionary antecedents of human joy? Physiology & Behavior.
- Winkler & Bryant (2021). Play vocalisations and human laughter. Bioacoustics.
- Provine (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation.
- Dunbar et al. (2012). Social laughter is correlated with an elevated pain threshold. Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
- Bryant et al. (2016). Detecting affiliation in colaughter across 24 societies. PNAS.

scenes.narration: In nineteen sixty-two, three schoolgirls started laughing.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character peeks through the window of an old brick school building on a rainy afternoon, curious.

scenes.narration: And they could not stop.
scenes.image_prompt: Three African schoolgirls in nineteen-sixties uniforms laughing helplessly at their desks in an old classroom.
scenes.fact_source: Rankin & Philip (1963). An epidemic of laughing in the Bukoba district of Tanganyika. Central African Journal of Medicine 9; Hempelmann (2007). Humor 20

scenes.narration: Within weeks, about ninety-five students were laughing.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands in a school corridor, eyes wide, as laughter fills every classroom.

scenes.narration: The school had to close its doors.
scenes.image_prompt: An old mission school with its wooden gate closed, empty yard, grey rainy sky.
scenes.fact_source: Rankin & Philip (1963). An epidemic of laughing in the Bukoba district of Tanganyika. Central African Journal of Medicine 9; Hempelmann (2007). Humor 20

scenes.narration: Then it spread to villages nearby. Like a cold.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character walks down a red dirt road between villages, looking back at houses where people laugh.

scenes.narration: Doctors found no poison, no germ, no infection.
scenes.image_prompt: A nineteen-sixties doctor examining notes at a wooden table in a village clinic, lamp light.
scenes.fact_source: Rankin & Philip (1963). An epidemic of laughing in the Bukoba district of Tanganyika. Central African Journal of Medicine 9; Hempelmann (2007). Humor 20

scenes.narration: You probably laughed today. Do you know why?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character laughs at a campfire with friends, then stops and looks puzzled at the viewer.

scenes.narration: Most laughs don't even follow a joke.
scenes.image_prompt: Two friends chatting at a cafe table and laughing at an ordinary moment, coffee cups between them.
scenes.fact_source: Provine, R. (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation. Viking

scenes.narration: By the end, you'll know what your laugh secretly says.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a glowing sound wave in his hands like a precious stone.

scenes.narration: And why laughter is older than humans themselves.
scenes.image_prompt: A young chimpanzee rolling on the forest floor, mouth open in a playful face, sunlight through trees.
scenes.fact_source: Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology 19, 1106-1111

scenes.narration: Here's a clue. Strangers can hear who your friends are.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character whispers behind his hand to the viewer, eyes narrowed playfully.

scenes.narration: Even rats make laugh-like sounds when tickled.
scenes.image_prompt: A small white rat lying on its back on a researcher's palm in a bright lab, looking happy.
scenes.fact_source: Bryant et al. (2016). Detecting affiliation in colaughter across 24 societies. PNAS 113, 4682-4687

scenes.narration: Imagine being a teacher that week.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands at the front of a classroom where every student is giggling, chalk in his hand, confused.

scenes.narration: Pupils sent home took the laughter with them to their villages.
scenes.image_prompt: Children walking home along a red dirt road between banana trees under a cloudy sky.
scenes.fact_source: Rankin & Philip (1963). An epidemic of laughing in the Bukoba district of Tanganyika. Central African Journal of Medicine 9; Hempelmann (2007). Humor 20

scenes.narration: Every family, every village, the same strange sound.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sits outside a village hut at dusk, hearing laughter from every direction.

scenes.narration: More than a dozen schools closed before it ended.
scenes.image_prompt: A row of empty wooden school desks in a quiet classroom, dust in the afternoon light.
scenes.fact_source: Rankin & Philip (1963). An epidemic of laughing in the Bukoba district of Tanganyika. Central African Journal of Medicine 9; Hempelmann (2007). Humor 20

scenes.narration: So let's find the very first laugh.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character walks into a misty green rainforest at dawn, pushing aside giant leaves.

scenes.narration: In two thousand nine, scientists tickled young apes and recorded the sounds.
scenes.image_prompt: A scientist gently tickling a baby orangutan in a sanctuary, both relaxed, sunlight through leaves.
scenes.fact_source: Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology 19, 1106-1111

scenes.narration: Yes. Tickling apes. For science.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character grins and wiggles his fingers like a tickle monster.

scenes.narration: Chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans all made breathy, panting laugh sounds.
scenes.image_prompt: Four young great apes playing together in a forest clearing, mouths open in play faces.
scenes.fact_source: Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology 19, 1106-1111

scenes.narration: Then they compared them with human babies laughing.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sits on the grass holding a giggling baby, both laughing.

scenes.narration: The pattern of the sounds matched the family tree of the apes.
scenes.image_prompt: A tree made of glowing sound waves with branches labelled by small ape faces, no letters.
scenes.fact_source: Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology 19, 1106-1111

scenes.narration: The closer the cousin, the closer the laugh.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands beside a chimpanzee, both laughing with the same open mouth.

scenes.narration: So laughter likely goes back at least ten million years.
scenes.image_prompt: A misty ancient forest at dawn with a primitive ape ancestor sitting on a branch.
scenes.fact_source: Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology 19, 1106-1111

scenes.narration: Ten million years. Before stone tools. Before fire.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a stone tool and a torch, then sets them down, amazed.

scenes.narration: Long before anyone told a single joke.
scenes.image_prompt: An empty prehistoric forest clearing at sunset with birds flying overhead.
scenes.fact_source: Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology 19, 1106-1111

scenes.narration: So laughing came first. Humour came much later.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character taps his head and smiles, as if a puzzle clicked.

scenes.narration: Ape laughs pant in and out. Ours mostly flows on the out-breath.
scenes.image_prompt: Two sound waves side by side floating over a forest pond, one short and choppy, one smooth.
scenes.fact_source: Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology 19, 1106-1111

scenes.narration: Our laugh is basically an upgraded ape laugh.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character laughs loudly with his head thrown back, like a cartoon.

scenes.narration: The change likely happened after our line split from chimpanzees.
scenes.image_prompt: A forest path splitting in two at dawn, apes walking one way, early humans the other.
scenes.fact_source: Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology 19, 1106-1111

scenes.narration: Somewhere along the way, we learned to laugh out loud.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character laughs with a group of early humans around a campfire at night.

scenes.narration: That split is usually placed around five to six million years ago.
scenes.image_prompt: Early upright humans walking across a grassy savanna at sunrise, long shadows.
scenes.fact_source: Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology 19, 1106-1111

scenes.narration: But wait. Are we the only ones laughing?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character raises an eyebrow at a group of animals watching him from the bushes.

scenes.narration: Neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp tickled young rats.
scenes.image_prompt: A smiling scientist in a white coat tickling a young rat on a lab table, warm lamp.
scenes.fact_source: Panksepp & Burgdorf (2003). 'Laughing' rats and the evolutionary antecedents of human joy? Physiology & Behavior 79, 533-547

scenes.narration: Imagine putting that on your resume.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a paper sign-shaped scroll and laughs, a tiny rat on his shoulder.

scenes.narration: The rats chirped at about fifty kilohertz, too high for human ears.
scenes.image_prompt: A glowing sound wave rising from a tiny rat into the dark air of a quiet lab.
scenes.fact_source: Panksepp & Burgdorf (2003). 'Laughing' rats and the evolutionary antecedents of human joy? Physiology & Behavior 79, 533-547

scenes.narration: A tiny laugh we can't even hear.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character cups his ear toward a small rat, straining to hear.

scenes.narration: They chased the tickling hand and came back for more.
scenes.image_prompt: A young rat running happily toward a gloved hand on a clean lab table.
scenes.fact_source: Panksepp & Burgdorf (2003). 'Laughing' rats and the evolutionary antecedents of human joy? Physiology & Behavior 79, 533-547

scenes.narration: Panksepp thought this was a kind of joy.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character smiles warmly, watching rats play in a box of wood shavings.

scenes.narration: Not everyone agrees it's laughter. But it looks a lot like play.
scenes.image_prompt: Two young rats wrestling playfully in wood shavings under soft light.
scenes.fact_source: Panksepp & Burgdorf (2003). 'Laughing' rats and the evolutionary antecedents of human joy? Physiology & Behavior 79, 533-547

scenes.narration: Panksepp even noticed the rats picked favourites.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds two tiny rats who both stretch toward his hand.

scenes.narration: Rats tickled often chirped more when that same hand came near.
scenes.image_prompt: A young rat standing on its hind legs reaching toward a gloved hand on a clean table.
scenes.fact_source: Panksepp & Burgdorf (2003). 'Laughing' rats and the evolutionary antecedents of human joy? Physiology & Behavior 79, 533-547

scenes.narration: A rat with a best friend. I love that.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character smiles softly at a rat sleeping in his palm.

scenes.narration: Young animals play most, and laugh most, in safe places.
scenes.image_prompt: Fox cubs tumbling over each other outside their den in soft morning light.
scenes.fact_source: Winkler & Bryant (2021). Play vocalisations and human laughter: a comparative review. Bioacoustics 30, 499-526

scenes.narration: And rats aren't alone.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sits in a meadow surrounded by playful animals.

scenes.narration: A review found play sounds in at least sixty-five species.
scenes.image_prompt: A collage-like meadow with puppies, monkeys, dolphins jumping in a lake and birds, all playing.
scenes.fact_source: Winkler & Bryant (2021). Play vocalisations and human laughter: a comparative review. Bioacoustics 30, 499-526

scenes.narration: Dogs pant when they play. Dolphins whistle.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character plays tug of war with a happy dog on a beach.

scenes.narration: Even three kinds of birds, including the kea parrot.
scenes.image_prompt: A green kea parrot rolling playfully in snow on a mountain, beak open.
scenes.fact_source: Winkler & Bryant (2021). Play vocalisations and human laughter: a comparative review. Bioacoustics 30, 499-526

scenes.narration: A parrot that laughs in the snow. Honestly, goals.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character lies in the snow laughing next to a kea parrot.

scenes.narration: These sounds mean one thing: this is play, not a fight.
scenes.image_prompt: Two wolf pups play-biting each other in tall grass, tails wagging.
scenes.fact_source: Winkler & Bryant (2021). Play vocalisations and human laughter: a comparative review. Bioacoustics 30, 499-526

scenes.narration: Quick test. Try tickling yourself right now.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character tries to tickle his own ribs, then frowns, completely unimpressed.

scenes.narration: Almost nobody can. Scientists found out why in nineteen ninety-eight.
scenes.image_prompt: A researcher adjusting a small robotic arm with a soft foam tip in a quiet lab.
scenes.fact_source: Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith (1998). Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation. Nature Neuroscience 1, 635-640

scenes.narration: Nothing. Not even a giggle. Rude.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character crosses his arms and pouts at his own hand.

scenes.narration: Your brain predicts the touch before your fingers even arrive.
scenes.image_prompt: A glowing brain with a bright spot at the back, small arrows pointing to a hand.
scenes.fact_source: Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith (1998). Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation. Nature Neuroscience 1, 635-640

scenes.narration: It's like a magician who knows the trick.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character pulls a rabbit from a hat and yawns, bored.

scenes.narration: A part called the cerebellum dampens the feeling of your own touch.
scenes.image_prompt: The back of a glowing transparent head with the small cerebellum lit in soft blue.
scenes.fact_source: Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith (1998). Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation. Nature Neuroscience 1, 635-640

scenes.narration: But when someone else does it, surprise wins.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character bursts out laughing as a friend tickles him from behind.

scenes.narration: When a machine added a tiny delay, people's own touch tickled more.
scenes.image_prompt: A soft foam paddle moving slowly over a person's palm, a small clock beside it.
scenes.fact_source: Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith (1998). Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation. Nature Neuroscience 1, 635-640

scenes.narration: So tickling needs two. It was always a social game.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character and a child tickle each other on a blanket by the river, both laughing.

scenes.narration: Just like apes tickling their young in the forest.
scenes.image_prompt: A mother chimpanzee tickling her baby on a mossy log, both with open play faces.
scenes.fact_source: Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology 19, 1106-1111

scenes.narration: Now picture an ancient camp.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sits among early humans in a cave camp at dusk, a fire crackling.

scenes.narration: Early humans lived in small groups that depended on each other.
scenes.image_prompt: A small band of early humans sharing food around a fire in front of a cave at dusk.
scenes.fact_source: Winkler & Bryant (2021). Play vocalisations and human laughter: a comparative review. Bioacoustics 30, 499-526

scenes.narration: Two young hunters wrestle. It looks dangerous.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character and a friend wrestle on the grass, both grinning.

scenes.narration: A laugh during rough play signals: relax, it's a game.
scenes.image_prompt: Two early human boys wrestling playfully while elders smile nearby, sunset light.
scenes.fact_source: Winkler & Bryant (2021). Play vocalisations and human laughter: a comparative review. Bioacoustics 30, 499-526

scenes.narration: Without that laugh, play-fighting could turn into real fighting.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds up his hands, laughing, as his friend pretends to punch him.

scenes.narration: Scientists see laughter as a signal that grew out of play.
scenes.image_prompt: Young chimpanzees chasing each other around a tree trunk with open play faces.
scenes.fact_source: Winkler & Bryant (2021). Play vocalisations and human laughter: a comparative review. Bioacoustics 30, 499-526

scenes.narration: A laugh was like a white flag. Peace. We're friends.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character waves a big leaf like a flag, laughing with the group.

scenes.narration: And it worked best in a crowd.
scenes.image_prompt: A crowd of early humans laughing together around a big fire at night, sparks rising.
scenes.fact_source: Provine, R. (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation. Viking

scenes.narration: Quick pause. If you're enjoying this, subscribe and stay with me. We'll keep exploring the ancient world together, one question at a time. It's free, it takes one second, and it helps more curious people find us.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character waves warmly at the viewer beside a campfire under a starry sky.

scenes.narration: Back to the crowd. Because laughter is mostly social.
scenes.image_prompt: A busy city street at night in light rain with groups of friends laughing under umbrellas.
scenes.fact_source: Provine, R. (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation. Viking

scenes.narration: Robert Provine spent years just watching people laugh.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sits on a park bench with a notebook, secretly watching people laugh.

scenes.narration: His students kept laughter diaries for a week.
scenes.image_prompt: A student writing in a small notebook on a bus at dusk, rain on the window.
scenes.fact_source: Provine, R. (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation. Viking

scenes.narration: Every laugh, every place, every person.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character scribbles tally marks on a cave wall with charcoal, laughing.

scenes.narration: They laughed about thirty times more with others than alone.
scenes.image_prompt: A lonely student in a dark room next to the same student laughing with friends in a bright kitchen.
scenes.fact_source: Provine, R. (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation. Viking

scenes.narration: Thirty times! Alone, we barely laugh at all.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sits alone in a quiet cave, unsmiling, then a friend arrives and he bursts out laughing.

scenes.narration: Even the person telling a story laughs more than the listeners.
scenes.image_prompt: A woman telling a story at a dinner table while laughing, friends smiling politely around her.
scenes.fact_source: Provine, R. (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation. Viking

scenes.narration: About forty-six percent more. We laugh at our own stories.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character tells a story by the fire, laughing hardest at his own joke while others smile.

scenes.narration: And most laughs follow ordinary lines like, see you later.
scenes.image_prompt: Two coworkers laughing while saying goodbye at an office door, evening light.
scenes.fact_source: Provine, R. (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation. Viking

scenes.narration: So laughing isn't about being funny. It's about being together.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character puts an arm around a friend's shoulder at the campfire, both laughing.

scenes.narration: Laughter tells the group: we're fine, we're on the same side.
scenes.image_prompt: A family laughing together around a table in a cozy home during a rainy evening.
scenes.fact_source: Provine, R. (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation. Viking

scenes.narration: So when did humour finally show up?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character scratches his head in front of a wall of ancient clay tablets.

scenes.narration: In two thousand eight, researchers hunted for the oldest recorded joke.
scenes.image_prompt: A historian reading old clay tablets with a magnifying glass in a museum basement.
scenes.fact_source: McDonald (2008). The world's oldest jokes, University of Wolverhampton (Sumerian proverb, about 1900 BCE; Westcar Papyrus riddle)

scenes.narration: Something deep. Philosophical. Wise.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character strokes an imaginary beard, trying to look wise.

scenes.narration: It came from Sumer, at least about four thousand years ago.
scenes.image_prompt: An ancient Sumerian city by a river at sunset, mud-brick walls glowing orange.
scenes.fact_source: McDonald (2008). The world's oldest jokes, University of Wolverhampton (Sumerian proverb, about 1900 BCE; Westcar Papyrus riddle)

scenes.narration: And the joke was about... someone passing gas.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character covers his mouth, trying hard not to laugh.

scenes.narration: A young wife breaking wind in her husband's lap. That was the punchline.
scenes.image_prompt: Two Sumerian scribes laughing over a clay tablet in lamp light, hands on their bellies.
scenes.fact_source: McDonald (2008). The world's oldest jokes, University of Wolverhampton (Sumerian proverb, about 1900 BCE; Westcar Papyrus riddle)

scenes.narration: Four thousand years, and fart jokes still work.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character laughs so hard he falls off a stone bench.

scenes.narration: Second on the list: an Egyptian riddle from an old papyrus.
scenes.image_prompt: An ancient Egyptian papyrus scroll on a wooden table, a lamp and a reed pen beside it.
scenes.fact_source: McDonald (2008). The world's oldest jokes, University of Wolverhampton (Sumerian proverb, about 1900 BCE; Westcar Papyrus riddle)

scenes.narration: Our humour got fancier. Our laugh stayed ancient.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a clay tablet in one hand and a smartphone in the other, smiling.

scenes.narration: Laughing came millions of years first. Jokes are the new part.
scenes.image_prompt: A long timeline drawn in the sand on a beach, a tiny clay tablet at the very end.
scenes.fact_source: Davila Ross, Owren & Zimmermann (2009). Reconstructing the evolution of laughter in great apes and humans. Current Biology 19, 1106-1111

scenes.narration: Here's something you never noticed about your own laugh.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character pauses mid-sentence at a dinner table, finger raised.

scenes.narration: Provine found we almost never laugh in the middle of a sentence.
scenes.image_prompt: Two friends talking on a park bench, speech bubbles without letters floating between them.
scenes.fact_source: Provine, R. (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation. Viking

scenes.narration: We wait for the pause. Like a full stop in speech.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character speaks, stops, then laughs, like punctuation.

scenes.narration: He called it the punctuation effect.
scenes.image_prompt: A row of glowing dots and pauses floating in the air between two laughing people at night.
scenes.fact_source: Provine, R. (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation. Viking

scenes.narration: Your brain schedules your laughs without asking you.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character looks at a tiny clock inside a glass head, amazed.

scenes.narration: Laughter and speech share the same breath, so they take turns.
scenes.image_prompt: A misty breath cloud from a laughing person on a cold autumn evening, street lamp glowing.
scenes.fact_source: Provine, R. (2000). Laughter: A Scientific Investigation. Viking

scenes.narration: And here's where it gets strange.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character leans toward the viewer, eyebrows raised mysteriously.

scenes.narration: In twenty twelve, Robin Dunbar's team made people laugh, then tested pain.
scenes.image_prompt: A row of people in a theatre laughing at a comedy show, warm stage light.
scenes.fact_source: Dunbar et al. (2012). Social laughter is correlated with an elevated pain threshold. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 279, 1161-1167

scenes.narration: They used things like a tight cuff on the arm.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character winces at a blood pressure cuff on his arm, then laughs.

scenes.narration: After laughing together, people put up with more discomfort.
scenes.image_prompt: A smiling volunteer in a lab with a frozen sleeve on her arm, a clock on the wall.
scenes.fact_source: Dunbar et al. (2012). Social laughter is correlated with an elevated pain threshold. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 279, 1161-1167

scenes.narration: Laughing made them tougher. At least for a while.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character flexes his arm proudly while still giggling.

scenes.narration: The researchers suspect the body's own endorphins are involved.
scenes.image_prompt: Glowing particles flowing through a calm human silhouette in the dark, soft blue light.
scenes.fact_source: Dunbar et al. (2012). Social laughter is correlated with an elevated pain threshold. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 279, 1161-1167

scenes.narration: Endorphins are the same family of chemicals as feel-good runner's high.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character jogs along a riverbank at sunrise, smiling.

scenes.narration: It's a link, not proof. Endorphins weren't measured directly.
scenes.image_prompt: Two scientists at a laptop looking at charts, a whiteboard behind them, coffee mugs.
scenes.fact_source: Dunbar et al. (2012). Social laughter is correlated with an elevated pain threshold. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 279, 1161-1167

scenes.narration: But for ancient humans, a warm group feeling mattered a lot.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sits shoulder to shoulder with his tribe in a cave during a storm.

scenes.narration: Dunbar thinks laughter helped bond groups too big for one-on-one grooming.
scenes.image_prompt: Monkeys grooming each other on a branch while a big group of early humans laughs below.
scenes.fact_source: Dunbar et al. (2012). Social laughter is correlated with an elevated pain threshold. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 279, 1161-1167

scenes.narration: Monkeys groom one friend at a time. We laugh with ten.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character laughs with ten people at once around a huge fire.

scenes.narration: A shared laugh reaches many people at the same moment.
scenes.image_prompt: A large outdoor gathering at night with lanterns and everyone laughing together.
scenes.fact_source: Dunbar et al. (2012). Social laughter is correlated with an elevated pain threshold. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 279, 1161-1167

scenes.narration: Remember the clue? Strangers can hear who your friends are.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds up a finger, remembering, in front of a cafe window.

scenes.narration: In twenty sixteen, researchers recorded pairs laughing together.
scenes.image_prompt: Two university students laughing together into a microphone in a small recording room.
scenes.fact_source: Bryant et al. (2016). Detecting affiliation in colaughter across 24 societies. PNAS 113, 4682-4687

scenes.narration: Some pairs were old friends. Some had just met.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands between two pairs of people, one hugging, one shaking hands awkwardly.

scenes.narration: Then nine hundred sixty-six people in twenty-four societies listened.
scenes.image_prompt: People of many cultures wearing headphones in villages, cities and markets around the world.
scenes.fact_source: Bryant et al. (2016). Detecting affiliation in colaughter across 24 societies. PNAS 113, 4682-4687

scenes.narration: From farmers to students. Different languages. Same test.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character wears headphones in a rice field, listening carefully.
